core: WHO working definition: social determinants of health are the conditions where people are born, grow, live, work, and age, plus the wider forces that shape daily life (with access to power, money, and resources)
six working domains, each with one line and an original example: neighborhood and built environment, education, income and jobs, food access, social context, health care access

why they matter: these non-medical conditions help drive patterns in health outcomes; the WHO states most of our health is determined by these root causes and that they can outweigh genetic influences or health care access
the social gradient: health improves step by step with advantage at every level of income (WHO)
determinants and disparities: unequal conditions produce unequal outcomes (link only; health-disparities is the sibling topic)
the honest framing: the ZIP code slogan is a simplification with a real core
supporting: CDC has adopted the WHO definition of social determinants of health

Healthy People 2030 groups SDOH into five official domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context
Healthy People 2030 lists SDOH examples: safe housing, transportation, neighborhoods; polluted air and water; access to nutritious foods; language and literacy skills
the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health issued the 2008 report Closing the gap in a generation
'upstream factors' terminology used by Healthy People 2030 for conditions usually unrelated to health care delivery

health equity: fairness and corrective action (owned by public-health:foundations:health-equity)
population health: aggregate health of groups and its measurement (owned by public-health:foundations:population-health)

claims.claim: The WHO defines social determinants of health as the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider forces that shape the conditions of daily life; its health-topics page adds people's access to power, money, and resources.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has adopted the WHO definition of social determinants of health and describes them as the nonmedical factors that influence health outcomes.

Healthy People 2030 (HHS) defines SDOH as the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age, and groups them into five official domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context.

Most of our health is determined by non-medical root causes of ill health, which include quality education, access to nutritious food, and decent housing and working conditions; research shows these social determinants can outweigh genetic influences or health care access in influencing health outcomes.

At all levels of income, health and illness follow a social gradient: the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health — the pattern is step by step, not only between the richest and the poorest.

The WHO's Commission on Social Determinants of Health issued a final report in 2008, Closing the gap in a generation: health equity through action on the social determinants of health, and the WHO health-topics page identifies three areas for critical action from that report, including tackling the inequitable distribution of power, money, and resources.

Social determinants of health also contribute to wide health disparities and inequities; for example, people who do not have access to grocery stores with healthy foods are less likely to have good nutrition, which raises their risk of conditions like heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.

There is growing recognition that zip code is understood to be a stronger predictor of a person's health than their genetic code; the honest reading is that this is shorthand for a bundle of neighborhood conditions strongly associated with health, not a literal claim that genetics or medical care do not matter.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 'ZIP code beats genetic code' slogan: literal claim vs shorthand
positions: Popular framing: 'your zip code is a stronger predictor of your health than your genetic code' (KFF notes the growing recognition of this relationship)

Precise view: ZIP codes are postal delivery routes, not neighborhoods; genetics and medical care remain powerful influences; the WHO's 'outweigh' statement is about relative influence on group patterns, not a claim that genes are irrelevant
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents the slogan as a simplification with a real core: place conditions bundle housing, jobs, food, safety, and schools that are strongly associated with health, while genetics and medical care still matter.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Number of SDOH domains: six working categories vs five official domains
positions: This lesson names six working categories (neighborhood and built environment, education, income and jobs, food access, social context, health care access) for teaching clarity

Healthy People 2030's official framework has five domains (economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context), and food access is not one of the five names
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states both: it presents six working categories and explicitly notes that the official Healthy People 2030 framework groups the same conditions into five domains, folding food access into categories such as economic stability.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much health is 'determined' by social determinants
positions: WHO fact sheet: 'Most of our health is determined by these non-medical root causes of ill health'
A literal reading could imply medical care is unimportant; the WHO's own phrasing is about relative influence ('can outweigh genetic influences or health-care access'), not zero-sum replacement
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states the WHO claim factually and adds an explicit caution that 'outweigh' does not mean 'replace' — genetics and medical care remain powerful influences.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft (public/content/phase-4/lessons.json) contained only generic boilerplate — 'Social Determinants Of Health is a foundational concept in Public Health', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer' — with no factual claims about social determinants of health, so there were no substantive claims to preserve or refute.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's boilerplate definition, objectives, vocabulary, and Eli-10 with WHO/CDC/HHS-verified content: the WHO working definition, six domain categories with original examples, the social gradient, the determinants-disparities link, and the ZIP code honest framing.

The draft framed the topic as 'a concept to organize information'; the lesson reframes it as a working definition with named domains and a factual account of why daily-life conditions matter, attributed to WHO, CDC, and Healthy People 2030.
The draft's Eli-10 'toolbox drawer' analogy was replaced with an original garden/watering-can analogy plus a statement of where it breaks down.
rightsIssues: None. WHO pages and the WHO Commission report are used as reference only, with facts synthesized in original wording and no source prose reproduced; CDC and HHS/Healthy People 2030 are U.S. government works (public domain, attributed); the KFF issue brief is used as reference only.
